text: In the autumn of 1950 the war in Korea seemed almost over. American and South Korean troops had smashed the North Korean army after the landing at Inchon. They had taken Pyongyang. Now they were racing north toward the Yalu River and the border with China. General Douglas MacArthur was confident. Word spread through the ranks that the boys would be home by Christmas. On November twenty-fourth he launched what he believed would be the final offensive of the war. On the eastern side of the peninsula the job fell to Ten Corps. At its spearhead was the First Marine Division. Fifteen thousand men under Major General Oliver Prince Smith. Their road led north from the port of Hungnam into the high country around a man-made lake the Americans called the Chosin Reservoir. Smith did not like what he saw. His division was being strung out along a single narrow road. Seventy-eight miles of dirt and gravel climbed from the coast into mountains more than four thousand feet high. One road in. One road out. The planners called it the Main Supply Route. The Marines simply called it the MSR. His corps commander Major General Edward Almond wanted speed. Smith wanted caution. So he quietly slowed his advance. He stockpiled ammunition at a mountain village called Hagaru-ri. He ordered his engineers to begin cutting an airstrip into the frozen ground. Some officers thought he was being timid. Within days that caution would save his division. Because the mountains were not empty. Since October an entire Chinese army group had been slipping across the Yalu. The Ninth Army Group under General Song Shilun. Twelve divisions. Roughly one hundred twenty thousand men. They marched at night. They hid in villages and forests by day. They lit no fires. American reconnaissance planes flew over the same ridges again and again and saw nothing. There had been warnings. In early November the Seventh Marines fought a sharp battle near a village called Sudong against Chinese troops. Prisoners were taken. They said many more were coming. But in Tokyo MacArthur's headquarters did not believe China would intervene in force. Mao Zedong had a different plan. He did not want to push the Americans back. He wanted to destroy them. Let the Marines climb deep into the mountains. Let them stretch their line thin along that single road. Then cut it into pieces and annihilate each piece one by one. By the last week of November the trap was set. The Fifth and Seventh Marines had pushed west of the reservoir to a cluster of huts called Yudam-ni. Behind them small garrisons held Hagaru-ri and Koto-ri. East of the reservoir an Army regimental combat team was moving into position. And all around them in the snow lay one hundred twenty thousand men waiting for the signal. Then the temperature began to fall.
